newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-India hangmen learn the ropes from fathers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-India hangmen learn the ropes from fathers.

text.p: Like other self-respecting professionals, Nata Mullick takes pride in a job well done.
"The Mullicks are known for doing a professional job. Not a single miss has been reported in three generations," he says.
Mullick, like his father and grandfather, is a hangman.
"When I undertake a job, the hanged body stays intact. No blood oozes out of the nose or ears or mouth. The eyes, however, become bloodshot," he says.
Mullick, 71, personally executes all condemned prisoners in eastern India and says he has hanged 24 people in his career. He says he now plans to teach his son the ropes.
Mullick's family is one of the handful of surviving clans of hangmen in India who pass their skills from generation to generation.
In northern India, Mamu Singh's family has been handling the gallows for more than half a century. Family members still travel across the region whenever an execution has to be carried out.
His elder brother Kallu, in his late 80s, says he has executed more than 200 people.
Mamu Singh, Kallu and his son Chilwa Ram jointly handled the hangings in 1989 of Satwant Singh and Kehar Singh, the assassins of prime minister Indira Gandhi.

"Whenever I get the message from the jail superintendent of Meerut asking me to go on assignment, either I take up the assignment myself or recommend either Chilwa Ram or Mamu to do the job. All of us are known for our efficiency," Kallu says.
Mamu Singh's son Rakesh carried out his first hanging in the western city of Jaipur in April when he and his father executed a murderer of four people.
INVOKE A GODDESS, PULL A LEVER AND IT'S OVER

"We invoke a goddess and then waste no time in pulling the lever," Mamu Singh told Reuters three hours after the hanging. He smelled of cheap country liquor, but his 24-year-old son was sober and looked subdued.
"We derive enormous strength from invoking her. It is that strength that helps in pulling the lever.

"Then the plank under the convict's feet goes down and the body starts shaking in the air, like a fish out of water. It shakes furiously for 15 or 20 seconds -- it depends on his weight and body structure," Singh explained animatedly.
The family carries their own Manila hemp rope for each execution. It is later packed away and reused.
"We know each fibre of the rope and so tying the knot is not a problem. It is a time-tested rope," Singh said.
Mullick says he uses soap and oil to keep his ropes soft.
The hangmen say each convict reacts differently as he approaches the noose.
"Some cry very badly. Sometimes we have to struggle, which is why two or three of us go along. Some abuse and curse and kick," Singh said. "And some are already half dead by the time they get there."
"Kehar Singh was reciting hymns when we hanged him."
VERY LITTLE WORK THESE DAYS
The death penalty in India is supposed to be awarded only in "rare cases of exceptional depravity and brutality", and the president can grant pardons to inmates on death row.

"In India, poverty, race and chance play roles in the outcome of capital cases and in the final decision as to who should live and who should not," Rajasthan state's inspector-general of jails Arun Dugar told Reuters.
"Studies the world over have found that the percentage of poor persons being awarded the death penalty is much higher than in cases of others," he said.
Capital punishment is seldom imposed in India any more, and life imprisonment or life is normally the maximum penalty, he added.
Unlike his grandfather Mishri Lal and father Shiv Lal, Mullick is not a full-time government employee, and says time hangs heavy on his hands these days.
"There is no work now," he complains. "The last hanging was done way back in 1991."
"I get paid per job only," he adds. "For one hanging I am paid 5,000 rupees ($140) and a bottle of liquor to enable me to drink and forget about the act."

Executions are carried out by tying the hands and feet of the convict, whose head is already covered by a black hood, tightening the noose round the neck and pulling a lever that removes the platform from underneath the condemned person.
Mamu Singh says hanging is an art. "The man who performs the job has to ensure that the convict does not suffer for long and everything should be over in just few seconds," he said.
Rakesh says he works in a leather factory and has received some primary education. But his father says he never had second thoughts about inducting him into the family profession.
"We are not killers. We are sent by the god with a specific assignment to eliminate those who commit evil," said Singh.
"What is wrong with it? God has punished them and we are simply doing god's work."
